performed_via_github_app.description:
Codecov provides highly integrated tools to group, merge, archive and compare coverage reports. Whether your team is comparing changes in a pull request or reviewing a single commit, Codecov will improve the code review workflow and quality.

## Code coverage done right.®

1. Upload coverage reports from your CI builds.
2. Codecov merges all builds and languages into one beautiful coherent report.
3. Get commit statuses, pull request comments and coverage overlay via our browser extension.

When Codecov merges your uploads it keeps track of the CI provider (inc. build details) and user specified context, e.g. `#unittest` ~ `#smoketest` or `#oldcode` ~ `#newcode`. You can track the `#unittest` coverage independently of other groups. [Learn more here](
http://docs.codecov.io/docs/flags)

Through **Codecov's Browser Extension** reports overlay directly in GitHub UI to assist in code review in [Chrome](https://chrome.google.com/webstore/detail/codecov/gedikamndpbemklijjkncpnolildpbgo) or Firefox (https://addons.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/addon/codecov/)

*Highly detailed* **pull request comments** and *customizable* **commit statuses** will improve your team's workflow and code coverage incrementally.

**File backed configuration** all through the `codecov.yml`. 

## FAQ
- Do you **merge multiple uploads** to the same commit? **Yes**
- Do you **support multiple languages** in the same project? **Yes**
- Can you **group coverage reports** by project and/or test type? **Yes**
- How does **pricing** work? Only paid users can view reports and post statuses/comments.

body:
Since it came up while working on this branch: here's a way to use a **base16 colorscheme** as your Hazel theme, written as a Colors config slide. You paste one base16 scheme's 16 colours in as sRGB triples — each one a colour picker in the editor — and all 142 of Hazel's colours are derived from them, in four variants (light/dark × normal/high-contrast). This is based off a random colorscheme i found online. Two properties of base16 do the work: - `base00..base07` is ordered by **role**, not by lightness: `base00` is always the page background and `base05` always the default text, so a light scheme puts its lightest colour at `base00` and a dark scheme its darkest. Deriving everything *relative* to those two anchors means one function serves either polarity — and high contrast is that same function with the two ends pushed outward. - A dark scheme *is* a light scheme with that ramp reversed. Published base16 pairs are literally this (Solarized Light `base00` is Solarized Dark `base07`, and so on down, with the eight accents untouched), so the nine-line `flip` earns both polarities from a single input. The result is that a colour asks for a *contrast* rather than a lightness (`at(0.)` is the background, `at(1.)` is the default text), which is what lets the same derivation serve all four schemes. The derived ramps land within a few points of the lightnesses the hand-written schemes on this branch hardcode — e.g. light `T2/T3/T4` come out at 95.1/92.4/89.9 where the handwritten values are 94/91/88. The palette below is Solarized. Swap the 16 triples for any base16 scheme and the editor follows. > [!NOTE] > This isn't paste-and-go against this branch: it needs two small additions that aren't here — an `Rgb(Int, Int, Int)` colour constructor (so a palette can be authored in sRGB bytes and still ramp, mix and report its lightness) and a `color_lightness` builtin (so the program can place a colour relative to the scheme's own background and text). Posting it as a demo of where the config slide can go.
colors.hz — 439 lines ``` # ══ Colour scheme, derived from a base16 palette ═════════════════════ # # ONE base16 scheme goes in, as 16 sRGB triples -- open below as colour # # pickers. Every one of Hazel's 142 colours comes out of it, four ways. # # # # palette_of seeds + ramp lightnesses -> every derived colour # # theme_of colours + role overrides -> the theme the app reads # # theme_of_base16 a base16 scheme -> a whole Hazel theme # # last line picks one, per (dark_mode, high_contrast) # # # # base16 orders base00..base07 by ROLE, not by lightness: base00 is # # always the page background and base05 always the default text, so a # # light scheme puts its lightest colour at base00 and a dark scheme its # # darkest. Two consequences, and they are the whole trick: # # # # * Deriving everything RELATIVE to those two anchors means one # # function serves either polarity, and high contrast is that same # # function with the two ends pushed outward. # # * A dark scheme IS a light scheme with that ramp reversed. Published # # base16 pairs are literally this -- Solarized Light base00 is # # Solarized Dark base07, and so on down, with the eight accents # # untouched -- so `flip` below earns both polarities from one input. # let dark_mode = ^^check(false) in let high_contrast = ^^check(false) in # ── The input: one base16 scheme, in sRGB ───────────────────────────── # # Every swatch is a colour picker: click one to open the OKLCH plane, or # # its RGB tab to type bytes. Edits are written back as Rgb, so the # # palette stays in the units it was authored in. # let scheme = ( base00 = ^^color(Rgb(253, 246, 227)), base01 = ^^color(Rgb(238, 232, 213)), base02 = ^^color(Rgb(147, 161, 161)), base03 = ^^color(Rgb(131, 148, 150)), base04 = ^^color(Rgb(101, 123, 131)), base05 = ^^color(Rgb(88, 110, 117)), base06 = ^^color(Rgb(7, 54, 66)), base07 = ^^color(Rgb(0, 43, 54)), base08 = ^^color(Rgb(220, 50, 47)), base09 = ^^color(Rgb(203, 75, 22)), base0A = ^^color(Rgb(181, 137, 0)), base0B = ^^color(Rgb(133, 153, 0)), base0C = ^^color(Rgb(42, 161, 152)), base0D = ^^color(Rgb(38, 139, 210)), base0E = ^^color(Rgb(108, 113, 196)), base0F = ^^color(Rgb(211, 54, 130)) ) in # ── One scheme, both polarities ─────────────────────────────────────── # # Reverse the eight monotone steps and leave the accents alone: what was # # the background becomes the text and vice versa. # let flip = fun s -> ^^fold(( base00 = s.base07, base01 = s.base06, base02 = s.base05, base03 = s.base04, base04 = s.base03, base05 = s.base02, base06 = s.base01, base07 = s.base00, base08 = s.base08, base09 = s.base09, base0A = s.base0A, base0B = s.base0B, base0C = s.base0C, base0D = s.base0D, base0E = s.base0E, base0F = s.base0F )) in # ── Seeds and ramp lightnesses become colours ───────────────────────── # let palette_of = fun (seed, step) -> # PAT is needed twice (TPAT aliases it) and a tuple cannot refer to # # its own fields, so it is bound first. # let pat = color_rotate(seed.`TYP`, -75.) in ^^fold(( `NONE` = seed.`NONE`, `SAND` = seed.`SAND`, `STONE` = seed.`STONE`, `BLACK` = seed.`BLACK`, `BR1` = seed.`BR1`, `T1` = seed.`T1`, `Y0` = seed.`Y0`, `Y1` = seed.`Y1`, `Y2` = seed.`Y2`, `Y3` = seed.`Y3`, `R0` = seed.`R0`, `R1` = seed.`R1`, `R2` = seed.`R2`, `TYP` = seed.`TYP`, `LABEL` = seed.`LABEL`, `highlight-a` = seed.`highlight-a`, `G0` = seed.`G0`, `G1` = seed.`G1`, `G2` = seed.`G2`, `GB0` = seed.`GB0`, `GB1` = seed.`GB1`, `textarea-v-stripe` = seed.`textarea-v-stripe`, `textarea-h-stripe` = seed.`textarea-h-stripe`, `textarea-h-strip-selected` = seed.`textarea-h-strip-selected`, `SHADOW` = seed.`SHADOW`, `ERRHOLE` = seed.`ERRHOLE`, `CREASE` = seed.`CREASE`, `exp-ap` = seed.`exp-ap`, `pat-ap` = seed.`pat-ap`, `exp-base` = seed.`exp-base`, `pat-base` = seed.`pat-base`, `exp-shadow` = seed.`exp-shadow`, `pat-shadow` = seed.`pat-shadow`, `exp-ap-shadow` = seed.`exp-ap-shadow`, `exp-cell` = seed.`exp-cell`, `pat-cell` = seed.`pat-cell`, `main-base` = seed.`main-base`, `main-shadow` = seed.`main-shadow`, # Ramps: BR2-4 step off BR1, T2-4 off T1. The lightnesses come # # from `step` and INVERT between schemes -- in dark, more # # contrast means lighter. # `BR2` = color_with_lightness(seed.`BR1`, step.`BR2`), `BR3` = color_with_lightness(seed.`BR1`, step.`BR3`), `BR4` = color_with_lightness(seed.`BR1`, step.`BR4`), `T2` = color_with_lightness(seed.`T1`, step.`T2`), `T3` = color_with_lightness(seed.`T1`, @7h3kk1d what's the big picture for dataflow here? thinking about this in a perf context specifically. when a view renders, where does it get its color info from? does it have to go through a config slide or is there some kind of intermediate in-memory representation, which is then updated when config slides are changed?

> @7h3kk1d what's the big picture for dataflow here? thinking about this in a perf context specifically. when a view renders, where does it get its color info from? does it have to go through a config slide or is there some kind of intermediate in-memory representation, which is then updated when config slides are changed?

It updates the css variables using setProperty after evaluation. So the in memory representation is the property stat on the dom. It stores a copy in local storage so this can get run before app initialization so the loading screen and such have access to it as well.
